newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's "dry canal" to boost local builders.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's "dry canal" to boost local builders.

text.p: A consortium proposing to build a "dry canal" across Nicaragua has signed an agreement with the local construction industry to give it priority in the project's construction, a top consortium official said on Saturday.

General manager of the Canal Interoceanico de Nicaragua S.A. (CINN), Juan Carlos Rivas, told Reuters the agreement signed late on Friday with the Nicaraguan Chamber of Construction would give preference to local builders, services and professionals.
"What we are doing is ratifying our decision to use Nicaraguan companies in an intensive and preferential fashion," Rivas said.
The proposed "dry canal" is a 236 mile (377 km) rail system to transport container cargo across the Central American isthmus. It will complement the Panama Canal, he said.

The $1.4 billion project, the largest in Nicaraguan history, would include the construction of two new container ports and surrounding free-trade zones; it has major foreign backers, Rivas said. The project's $15 million feasibility study will begin in the first week of January and its results should be released by the end of October, he said.
If the study's results are approved by the Nicaraguan government, the railroad would take three additional years to build, Rivas said.

Rivas said President-elect Arnoldo Aleman, whose government takes office Jan. 10, has given the project its support. "The new government has formed a commission that is already functioning, headed by Jilberto Cuadra (a prominent local builder), to evaluate and keep him informed on the project," he said.
While there is skepticism about the plan outside of Nicaragua, the local business community is rallying around it.

The president of the Nicaraguan Chamber of Construction, Benjamin Lanzas, said there was a 90 percent probablity of the railroad being built. "The government is seriously committed to the project and the builders think it has enormous possibilities," Lanzas said.
